name: Battle of Mycale
info: Greek marines under the Spartan king Leotychides landed at Mount Mycale on the coast of Ionia in 479 BCE, routed the Persian force there and burned its fleet, helping to end Xerxes' invasion of Greece.

facts.date: 27 or 28 August 479 BCE, the afternoon of the same day as the Battle of Plataea according to Paul A. Rahe; Charles Hignett proposes late August
facts.place: The slopes of Mount Mycale on the coast of Ionia, opposite the island of Samos, in present-day Turkey; the exact site is disputed
facts.sides: An alliance of Greek city-states including Sparta, Athens and Corinth, under the Spartan king Leotychides, against the Persian Empire of Xerxes I, whose land force was led by Tigranes and whose fleet was led by Artaÿntes; the strengths on both sides are disputed
facts.outcome: The Persian troops were routed and their camp stormed, and the Persian ships were captured and burned. Tigranes and Mardontes were killed, while Artaÿntes and Ithamitres escaped.

t: The Persian fleet, probably fewer than a third of Herodotus's 300 ships after the Phoenician ships were dismissed, was beached below Mycale and fenced with a palisade, and the Greeks attacked it there by landing their marines.
The Ionian Greek contingents in the Persian army turned on the Persians during the fighting, though Joshua Nudell argues this betrayal is overstated and perhaps invented.
Together with Plataea, the battle ended the second Persian invasion of Greece, and the Greeks then went over to the offensive.
dyk: Richard Evans notes that Mycale was the first battle in recorded history fought on a beach, and he estimates that the strip of beach was only 20 to 30 metres long at low tide.
ev: A Persian army under Xerxes defeats the Greeks at Thermopylae and Artemisium, and the Greek navy wins at Salamis
The Greek fleet of about 110 ships gathers at Aegina under the Spartan king Leotychides and moves to Delos
A delegation from Samos tells the Greeks that the Ionian cities are ready to revolt, and the fleet sails for Samos
The Persians withdraw from Samos and beach their fleet below Mycale behind a palisaded camp
The Greeks land, defeat the Persian force and burn its ships
The Greek fleet sails to the Hellespont and finds the pontoon bridges destroyed, and the Athenians besiege Sestos
Chios, Lesbos and Samos join the Hellenic alliance

sections.background:
Xerxes I had invaded Greece in 480 BCE. His army defeated the Greeks at Thermopylae, and his fleet forced the Greek fleet to withdraw at Artemisium, after which the Persians burned Boeotian cities and took the evacuated city of Athens. At Salamis the Greek navy won a victory that prevented the conquest of the Peloponnese, and Xerxes retreated to Asia with a minor portion of his army, leaving Mardonius with most of it to finish the war the next year.

The Persian fleet was stationed at Samos to defend Ionia and avert an Ionian revolt. Its morale was breaking, and its crews were waiting anxiously for news of Mardonius. Charles Hignett argues that only a Persian victory on land in Greece could sustain Persian rule in Ionia. In the spring of 479 BCE the Greek fleet of about 110 ships lay at Aegina under the Spartan king Leotychides. Six people from Chios who had failed to overthrow their tyrant Strattis reached Sparta and persuaded the fleet to move to Delos, but the Greeks hesitated to go further.

In July a delegation from Samos under Hegesistratos told them that the Ionian cities were eager to revolt and that the Persian fleet was in poor repair. Leotychides and the council of war decided to take the chance and sailed for Samos. Historians differ on how risky this was: Hignett says Leotychides was gambling on a battle at a place the Persians would choose, while Jack Balcer stresses that the fleet's original task had only been to keep the Persian fleet from reinforcing Mardonius.
sections.forces:
Herodotus gives the Persian fleet that wintered at Cyme as 300 ships, but the Phoenician ships were dismissed before the battle. Hignett finds 300 too many even with the Phoenicians, and Peter Green and John Barron both estimate about 100 ships after their departure. Richard Evans, by contrast, estimates 200. Tigranes commanded the land force, and Artaÿntes was joint commander of the fleet and appointed his nephew Ithamitres as the third commander. Herodotus puts the Persian army at 60,000, which Hignett says his own narrative contradicts. Hignett and William Shepherd think Tigranes had about 10,000 men, Green 6,000 plus 4,000 marines from the fleet, and Evans about 4,000 Persian combatants in all. Shepherd notes that he had no cavalry.

Andrew Robert Burn estimates 110 Greek ships and notes that the figure of 250 is given only by Ephorus. Herodotus gives no order of battle. Shepherd thinks Athens supplied a third of the ships, and Evans reckons 70 Athenian, 8 Spartan, 20 Corinthian, 3 Troezenian and 8 Sicyonian. Estimates of the marines run from 2,000 to 3,000 (George Cawkwell) to 3,300 (Michael Flower and John Marincola, and Hignett). Shepherd allows at most 25,000 Greek soldiers, most of them oarsmen serving as light infantry, while Evans counts 1,100 hoplites. Flower and Marincola think Leotychides and Xanthippus, the Athenian commander, probably had equal powers and decided by majority vote.

The Persians took the arms of the Samians in their army, whom they found unreliable, and sent the Milesians to guard the mountain passes, suspecting they wished to defect.
sections.course:
When the Persians heard that the Greek fleet was approaching, they sailed from Samos to Mycale, possibly because they had decided they could not fight at sea, and in the chaos the Samians freed 500 Athenian captives. The Persians beached their ships behind rocks, built abatis with recently cut wood, set stakes on the ramparts and expected a siege. The Greeks camped at Kalamoi, near the Heraion of Samos, then moved on Mycale, calling on the Ionians to revolt, and landed out of sight of the enemy. Herodotus reports a rumour that spread among them of a Greek victory at Plataea earlier that day.

The Greeks probably formed two wings. On the left stood the Athenians, Corinthians, Sicyonians and Troezenians, about half the army, between the shore and the foothills. On the right were the Spartans and the other contingents on rough ground in the hills. The left began fighting while the right was still crossing the hills. The Persians came out and set up a shield wall. Green argues that sending the Athenian flank forward alone was a ruse of Leotychides.

The Greek right, under heavy arrow fire, closed in, and its contingents broke the wall by shoving. Tigranes and Mardontes died, and the Persians fled to their camp. Most of the fugitives ran on, but the ethnic Persians stood and fought until the Greek left outflanked the camp and fell on their rear. Herodotus says the disarmed Samians then joined the Greeks, the other Ionian contingents followed, and the Milesians at the passes first misdirected the fleeing Persians and then killed them. The Greeks burned the Persian ships after a hard fight with the Persian marines, and the camp.
sections.aftermath:
Herodotus gives no figures for the dead, saying only that losses were heavy on both sides. The Sicyonians suffered especially and lost their general Perilaus. Green estimates the Persian dead at 4,000. Mardontes and Tigranes were killed, but Artaÿntes and Ithamitres escaped. Hermolycus of Athens was thought the most gallant Greek, and the Athenians were thought the most courageous contingent, followed by Corinth, Troezen and Sicyon. Burn and Muhammad Dandamayev hold that the destruction of the Persian fleet gave the Greek fleets complete freedom of movement, and Dandamayev says the Persian and Median marines and the Persians of Tigranes' army were almost completely massacred.

With Plataea and Mycale the second Persian invasion was over. The Greeks returned to Samos and then sailed to the Hellespont to break down the pontoon bridges, but found them destroyed. The Peloponnesians sailed home. The Athenians stayed to attack the Chersonesos and, after a long siege, took Sestos, the strongest town of the region. Chios, Lesbos and Samos joined the Hellenic alliance and their Persian garrisons were eliminated. The Greeks could not subdue Ionia entirely and freed only the Aegean islands, but Thrace and Macedonia broke with the Persians, as did the coastal areas of Lydia and the Greek communities from the Troad to Caria.

The Peloponnesians proposed moving the Ionian Greeks to northern Greece and giving them the lands of the medizers, but the plan was dropped, and Xanthippus said Athens would not let its settlements be abandoned.
sections.sources:
The main source is Herodotus, who tells the battle in Book Nine of his Histories. Diodorus Siculus also gives an account, which Flower and Marincola find unreliable and mixed with the claims of his main source, Ephorus of Cyme. Most ancient writers gave the battle little thought. Plutarch is the only one to describe the Athenians as proud of it, and he notes Corinthian gallantry. Thucydides did not rate it as highly as Salamis or Artemisium.

Modern historians have found Herodotus's account shaped by its design. Detlev Fehling and Shepherd note its likeness to Plataea, and others compare it with Artemisium, Lade and Thermopylae. Hignett thinks the similarities natural. David Asheri holds that Herodotus told the battle from a religious rather than a military viewpoint, and Henry Immerwahr that its Athenian bias comes from a pro-Athenian source, probably Hellanicus of Lesbos. Evans suggests Homer's Iliad as a model. Nudell thinks the Ionian betrayal of the Persians may have been invented to save the reputation of Greek states that had fought for them.

The site is disputed, and proposals include Domatia (Theodor Wiegand), near Ak Bogaz (Johannes Kromayer), Atburgazı (Shepherd), Güllübahçe (Jan Zacharias van Rookhuijzen) and a place between Atburgazı and Yuvaca (Dietram Müller). Iain McDougall doubts that the Persian ships were burned, since ships were valuable loot, while Asheri says the Greeks lacked crews to man them.
sections.legacy:
Cawkwell calls the battle a very minor affair, but says its results were large because it led to an Ionian revolt, and Burn calls it relatively small. Iain Spence argues that it confirmed Greek command of the sea and that the defection of the Aegean states helped the Greek naval campaigns, leading to the Delian League and the naval empire of Athens. Persian borders were then fixed, and later Persian invasions became rare. Bury argues that Spartan indecision left the Greeks of Asia Minor to the Delian League under Athens, and that the Spartans' hesitation and Athenian resolve fed the rivalry of the fifth century BCE. Nudell sees in the debate over the Ionians a foreshadowing of the Peloponnesian War.

Spoils were displayed at Delphi, where the Athenians took credit in an inscription without naming their allies. Barron suggests that cables from the Persian bridges adorned the Temple of Athena Nike, and Demosthenes thought the statue of Athena Promachos was paid for by the loot of Plataea and Mycale. Vitruvius says masts and spars of the Persian ships went into the roof of the Odeon of Pericles.

Memory of the battle is uneven. Flower and Marincola note that no Athenian orator celebrated it, perhaps because a Spartan led it, and David C. Yates notes that Samos and Chios, with strong claims, are missing from the Serpent Column. An epigram from Megara tells of Megarians who fought and suffered losses, though no account of the battle names them.

summary: At Mycale in August 479 BCE a Greek force landed from its fleet under the Spartan king Leotychides and routed the Persian troops beached below the mountain, killing their commanders Tigranes and Mardontes and burning their ships. With Plataea it ended the second Persian invasion of Greece.
references: Peter Green, The Greco-Persian Wars (University of California Press, 1996)
Charles Hignett, Xerxes' Invasion of Greece (Clarendon Press, 1963)
John Francis Lazenby, The Defence of Greece, 490-479 B.C. (Aris & Phillips, 1993)
Andrew Robert Burn, Persia and the Greeks. The Defence of the West, c. 546-478 B. C. (Gerald Duckworth & Co., 1984)
Joshua P. Nudell, Accustomed to Obedience? Classical Ionia and the Aegean World, 480–294 BCE (University of Michigan Press, 2023)
Michael A. Flower, Herodotus. Histories Book IX (Cambridge University Press, 2002)
notes: Strengths are disputed throughout: Persian fleet 300 (Herodotus), about 100 (Green, Barron), 200 (Evans); land force 60,000 (Herodotus), 10,000, 6,000 plus 4,000 marines, 4,000; Greek ships 110 (Burn) or 250 (Ephorus). I give them all with attributions.

Left out as garbled or impossible: the article says that 'in the spring of 488 BC' Xenagoras of Halicarnassus, tyrant of Cilicia, raided Didyma in revenge for the Milesians changing sides at Mycale. A date nine years before the battle fits nothing. Also left out: the Bactrian revolt 'bolstering' Artabanus (thin), Masistes's accusation of cowardice, and the Phrynichus and Aeschylus remarks (garbled).
The article says the Greek and Persian fleets were off Delos while also saying Xanthippus's Athenian navy joined 'off Delos'; I wrote only that the fleet moved to Delos.
The takeaway 'probably fewer than a third of Herodotus's 300 ships' rests on the estimates of about 100 ships by Green and Barron; Evans estimates 200, which is given in the forces section.

The article's lead calls the victory 'decisive' and the destruction of the Persian navy 'complete', and says Plataea happened 'allegedly' the same day; I kept the same-day claim attributed to Rahe's dating.
Evans's wedge-formation reconstruction and the beach-length arithmetic are speculative and omitted apart from the beach length in the dyk.
The 'ev' entries for 479 BCE have no dates more exact than the article gives; the Samian delegation in July is the article's wording.
